questions.stem: An internationally qualified nurse is unsure whether a safeguarding concern must be reported directly to an external authority. What is the most professional action?

options.text: Consult local law, organisational policy and an appropriate senior clinician immediately.
Follow the reporting process used in the nurse's previous country.
Wait until definite proof is available.
Ask the family whether they want the concern reported.

questions.rationale: Mandatory-reporting duties vary between jurisdictions. Safe adaptation requires checking the local framework rather than relying on previous-country practice.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a professional code from a practice standard?

options.text: Codes are legally binding in every situation, while standards are optional.
Codes describe expected professional behaviour, while standards describe the level of practice required.
Standards apply only to managers.
There is no practical difference.

questions.rationale: Codes commonly describe conduct and values, while standards define expected professional performance.

questions.stem: An IQN is asked to perform a procedure that was within scope in a previous country but is unfamiliar under the new employer's policy. What should happen first?

options.text: Proceed because previous registration confirms competence.
Ask the patient to consent to the uncertainty.
Verify local scope, policy and supervision requirements before performing the procedure.
Delegate the procedure to another new employee.

questions.rationale: Previous experience does not automatically establish authority in a new regulatory and organisational system.

questions.stem: Which source most directly defines registration conditions and legal nursing authority?

options.text: Workplace custom.
A colleague's opinion.
The nurse's previous-country job description.
The local nursing regulator and applicable nurse-practice law.

questions.rationale: Registration conditions and nurse-practice law define legal authority and obligations.

questions.stem: A workplace policy conflicts with the nurse's professional judgement about immediate patient safety. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Protect the patient, seek urgent clarification and escalate through approved channels.
Follow policy without question.
Ignore the policy permanently.
Ask the patient to resolve the conflict.

questions.rationale: Policy supports practice but does not replace professional judgement or accountability.

questions.stem: Which situation may create a mandatory-reporting obligation, depending on local law?

options.text: A colleague requesting annual leave.
Suspected abuse, serious misconduct or impaired practice.
A patient refusing food.
A minor disagreement during handover.

questions.rationale: The notes identify suspected abuse, impaired practice, serious misconduct and communicable disease as possible reporting areas.

questions.stem: A nurse is unfamiliar with the local medication-checking process. What is the safest response?

options.text: Use the system from the previous workplace.
Avoid all medication administration indefinitely.
Complete orientation, review policy and request supervision until competent.
Ask another IQN to explain informally.

questions.rationale: Seeking clarification and supervised orientation are professional safety behaviours.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates personal accountability within an international team?

options.text: Assuming the team leader carries responsibility for all decisions.
Following established habits without question.
Avoiding documentation of uncertainty.
Understanding local expectations and accepting responsibility for one's own decisions and omissions.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability remains personal even when care is delivered by a team.

questions.stem: A nurse discovers that a local code requires disclosure of a conflict of interest. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the local code and seek guidance if the process is unclear.
Use the previous country's rules instead.
Disclose only if a patient complains.
Keep the matter private.

questions.rationale: IQNs must adapt to the local regulatory and professional framework.

questions.stem: Which action is most appropriate when a legal requirement is unclear during urgent care?

options.text: Delay all care until a lawyer is available.
Provide necessary safe care within scope while seeking immediate senior or specialist advice.
Rely on memory from previous practice.
Ask the patient's relative to decide.

questions.rationale: The nurse should protect safety, remain within scope and obtain timely advice.

questions.stem: A nurse is told, 'This is how we always do it here,' but the practice appears inconsistent with professional standards. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the custom as local policy.
Copy the practice to fit in.
Check the applicable standard and raise the concern respectfully.
Document the concern only after harm occurs.

questions.rationale: Workplace custom does not override professional standards or legal duties.

questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates successful regulatory adaptation?

options.text: The nurse performs all tasks independently within the first week.
The nurse continues previous-country routines.
The nurse avoids complex decisions.
The nurse understands local laws, standards, scope and reporting duties and seeks advice appropriately.

questions.rationale: Safe adaptation combines knowledge, verified scope and appropriate consultation.

questions.stem: An IQN notices a colleague showing signs of impairment while providing care. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Protect patients and follow local escalation and reporting requirements.
Wait until an error occurs.
Confront the colleague publicly.
Send an anonymous social-media message.

questions.rationale: Patient protection and local reporting processes take priority.

questions.stem: Which statement about organisational policy is correct?

options.text: Policy replaces professional judgement.
Policy provides local processes but must be interpreted alongside law, standards and patient needs.
Policy applies only to permanent employees.
Policy is optional for experienced nurses.

questions.rationale: Policies guide local practice but do not remove professional accountability.

questions.stem: A new nurse has completed orientation but remains unsure about one high-risk task. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Perform it independently to build confidence.
Ask the patient whether supervision is necessary.
Request supervised practice and competency verification.
Refuse to learn the task.

questions.rationale: Competence should be demonstrated, especially for unfamiliar or high-risk activities.

questions.stem: Which professional behaviour most protects the public?

options.text: Keeping uncertainty private.
Relying on senior staff to notice problems.
Avoiding unfamiliar patients.
Recognising limits, maintaining competence and reporting serious risks appropriately.

questions.rationale: Professional regulation is intended to maintain competence and protect the public.

questions.stem: A nurse learns that communicable-disease reporting differs locally. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review current local requirements and follow the designated pathway.
Use the process remembered from nursing school.
Leave reporting to the patient.
Share the diagnosis with all staff.

questions.rationale: Reporting requirements are jurisdiction-specific and must be verified.

questions.stem: What is the best reason for an IQN to seek clarification?

options.text: It shows lack of preparation.
It is a professional response when local systems, law or scope are uncertain.
It transfers accountability to the adviser.
It is required only during orientation.

questions.rationale: Seeking clarification supports safe practice and does not remove personal accountability.

questions.stem: A senior colleague instructs an IQN not to report a serious safety event. What should the IQN do?

options.text: Follow the senior colleague's instruction.
Wait until employment probation ends.
Use the approved escalation or reporting pathway despite hierarchy.
Discuss the event outside the organisation.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy does not remove legal and professional reporting obligations.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe international professional practice?

options.text: The nurse adapts previous habits only when convenient.
The nurse avoids asking questions.
The nurse relies on workplace tradition.
The nurse applies local law, standards, policy and professional judgement consistently.

questions.rationale: International practice requires deliberate adaptation to the local framework. Section 2 - Complex Consent, Capacity and Ethical Decision-Making

questions.stem: An older patient with fluctuating delirium refuses a procedure. What is the nurse's best initial action?

options.text: Assess and support communication, seek timely clinical review and recognise that capacity may fluctuate.
Assume the patient lacks capacity because delirium is present.
Ask the family to consent immediately.
Proceed because the procedure is beneficial.

questions.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific and may fluctuate. It should not be removed solely because delirium is present.

questions.stem: Which abilities are central to decision-making capacity?

options.text: Signing a form and agreeing with the clinician.
Understanding, retaining, weighing information and communicating a choice.
Remembering all previous treatment.
Having no mental-health diagnosis.

questions.rationale: These are the core functional elements described in the notes.

questions.stem: A patient understands information about a low-risk blood test but cannot understand a complex surgical decision. What principle applies?

options.text: Capacity is all-or-nothing.
The patient lacks capacity for all care.
Capacity is decision-specific.
Family consent is always required.

questions.rationale: A person may have capacity for one decision and not another.

questions.stem: Which action best supports decision-making before considering a substitute?

options.text: Ask the family to decide first.
Withhold difficult information.
Assume refusal indicates incapacity.
Use simpler language, an interpreter, visual aids or additional time.

questions.rationale: People should receive practical support to decide wherever possible.

questions.stem: A family requests treatment that conflicts with the patient's clearly documented prior wishes. What should guide the decision?

options.text: The patient's known wishes, values, applicable law and best interests.
The family's preference alone.
The most expensive option.
The opinion of the most senior relative.

questions.rationale: Substitute decisions should reflect the person's known values and lawful best-interest processes.

questions.stem: What is the first step in a structured ethical decision framework?

options.text: Choose the safest option immediately.
Identify the ethical problem and gather relevant facts.
Ask the family to vote.
Document the final decision.

questions.rationale: A transparent process begins by defining the problem and facts.

questions.stem: Which factor should be separated clearly during ethical reasoning?

options.text: Only the medical diagnosis.
Only the patient's preference.
Facts, stakeholder values, law, policy and professional obligations.
Only organisational cost.

questions.rationale: Structured reasoning distinguishes these elements before options are considered.

questions.stem: A patient refuses a beneficial treatment for cultural reasons. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the refusal is uninformed.
Ask family to override the refusal.
Document the patient as non-compliant.
Assess understanding, explore the person's values and respect the decision if capacity and voluntariness are present.

questions.rationale: Autonomy applies to informed decisions that professionals may not prefer.

questions.stem: When is ethics consultation most appropriate?

options.text: When complex or unresolved conflict remains after appropriate discussion and review.
For every routine consent.
Only after litigation begins.
When the nurse wants to transfer accountability.

questions.rationale: Senior, legal, ethics or specialist consultation may be needed when conflict remains unresolved.

questions.stem: A patient communicates a choice but cannot explain relevant risks or compare options. What should the nurse recognise?

options.text: Communication alone proves capacity.
Further assessment of understanding and weighing is required.
The choice must be accepted immediately.
The family should decide without assessment.

questions.rationale: Capacity requires more than expressing a preference.

questions.stem: Which documentation best supports a complex capacity decision?

options.text: The conclusion only.
The family's opinion only.
Information provided, supports used, the person's responses, consultation and reasoning.
A statement that the patient was confused.

questions.rationale: Transparent documentation should show the assessment and reasoning process.

questions.stem: A patient with fluctuating cognition is most alert in the morning. What should the team consider?

options.text: Assuming permanent incapacity.
Avoiding all consent discussions.
Using family consent automatically.
Making the decision at the person's best time where clinically possible.

questions.rationale: Timing may support the person's decision-making ability.

questions.stem: A substitute decision-maker requests an option that appears contrary to the patient's values. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Raise the concern and seek senior, legal or ethics review.
Follow the request automatically.
Ask another relative to decide.
Proceed without documentation.

questions.rationale: Substitute authority must be exercised lawfully and consistently with the person's wishes and interests.

questions.stem: Which statement about capacity is correct?

options.text: A diagnosis of dementia automatically removes capacity.
Capacity may fluctuate and should be assessed for the specific decision.
Only doctors may notice capacity concerns.
Refusal proves incapacity.

questions.rationale: Capacity cannot be assumed absent based on diagnosis or disagreement.

questions.stem: An urgent intervention is required and the patient's decision-making capacity cannot be assessed fully. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delay all care regardless of risk.
Ask any family member to sign.
Follow the applicable emergency legal and clinical process and document the circumstances.
Use the process from the nurse's previous country.

questions.rationale: Urgent care must follow local emergency law and policy.

questions.stem: Which approach best prevents coercion?

options.text: Presenting one option as the only responsible choice.
Using family pressure.
Withholding risks to reduce anxiety.
Providing balanced information and allowing voluntary choice.

questions.rationale: Voluntariness is an essential part of valid consent.

questions.stem: A patient needs an interpreter to understand a serious treatment decision. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange professional interpretation and reassess understanding.
Use a family member for convenience.
Proceed with written English information.
Assume nodding indicates consent.

questions.rationale: Communication support is necessary for meaningful consent.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates supported decision-making?

options.text: The family makes the decision quickly.
The person participates as fully as possible using tailored communication and assistance.
The clinician selects the least risky option.
The consent form is signed.

questions.rationale: Supported decision-making maximises the person's own participation.

questions.stem: A disagreement between family and team remains unresolved after several meetings. What is the next appropriate step?

options.text: Continue arguing informally.
Follow the family's preference.
Seek senior review, legal advice, ethics consultation or specialist support.
Discharge the patient.

questions.rationale: Unresolved complex conflict requires formal consultation.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects sound ethical decision-making?

options.text: The most senior clinician decides.
The family agrees.
The decision is made quickly.
Facts, values, law, policy and options are considered transparently and the reasoning is documented.

questions.rationale: A transparent, structured process is the defining feature. Section 3 - Delegation, Advocacy and Interprofessional Accountability

questions.stem: An IQN is asked to delegate a complex assessment to a worker whose local role excludes clinical judgement. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Decline, explain the scope concern and arrange an appropriate alternative assessment.
Delegate because the worker performed similar tasks overseas.
Ask the patient to accept the risk.
Delegate and review the result later.

questions.rationale: Titles and duties differ across systems; role boundaries must be verified locally.

questions.stem: Which factor is most important before delegating care?

options.text: Whether the task is convenient.
Patient stability, task complexity, local scope and the worker's competence.
The worker's confidence only.
The nurse's workload only.

questions.rationale: Safe delegation requires matching the task and circumstances to authorised competence.

questions.stem: How should supervision be adjusted?

options.text: Use the same level for every worker.
Supervision ends after the task is assigned.
Match direction, monitoring and follow-up to patient risk and worker competence.
Provide supervision only to students.

questions.rationale: Supervision should be proportionate to risk and capability.

questions.stem: A delegated worker reports a significant change in a patient's condition. What should the registered nurse do?

options.text: Ask the worker to decide the next step.
Wait for the next scheduled review.
Document the report only.
Reassess promptly and determine the required escalation.

questions.rationale: Assessment, judgement and evaluation remain nursing responsibilities.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates advocacy?

options.text: Clarifying information and challenging an unsafe order respectfully.
Avoiding disagreement with the team.
Making decisions without the patient.
Sharing concerns only after discharge.

questions.rationale: Advocacy may require respectful challenge to protect rights and safety.

questions.stem: A patient from a minority group receives dismissive responses to repeated pain reports. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the pattern reflects different communication style.
Assess the pain objectively, advocate for equitable care and escalate if required.
Ask the patient to be more assertive.
Wait for a formal complaint.

questions.rationale: Advocacy includes challenging discriminatory or unsafe care.

questions.stem: Which communication is most assertive?

options.text: 'You are wrong.'
'Do whatever you think.'
'I am concerned that the patient's condition is worsening. These are the changes, and I need urgent review.'
'This always happens on your shift.'

questions.rationale: Assertive communication is clear, factual, respectful and action-focused.

questions.stem: A colleague dismisses an IQN's safety concern because of hierarchy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Withdraw the concern.
Discuss the colleague on social media.
Ask the patient to complain.
Use structured communication and continue through the escalation pathway if unresolved.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy should not prevent escalation of safety concerns.

questions.stem: Which task is least appropriate to delegate?

options.text: Clinical interpretation of new deterioration.
Routine observations for a stable patient.
Assistance with hygiene.
Recording oral intake.

questions.rationale: Clinical judgement generally remains with the registered nurse.

questions.stem: A worker accepts a delegated task but has not used the equipment before. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Allow the worker to learn during the task.
Provide training or reassign the task to a competent person.
Ask the patient to supervise.
Proceed if the worker signs responsibility.

questions.rationale: Competence must be established before delegation.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective supervision?

options.text: The task is completed.
The nurse saves time.
The worker receives clear direction, changes are reported and the nurse evaluates the outcome.
The worker accepts legal accountability.

questions.rationale: Completion alone does not demonstrate safe supervision.

questions.stem: A patient needs help navigating several unfamiliar services. What is the nurse's advocacy role?

options.text: Refer the patient without explanation.
Choose services without consultation.
Ask the family to manage alone.
Clarify pathways, support communication and help coordinate access.

questions.rationale: Advocacy includes helping people navigate complex systems.

questions.stem: A nurse disagrees with a medical plan but has incomplete information. What should happen first?

options.text: Clarify the facts and rationale before escalating the concern.
Reject the plan.
Tell the patient the plan is unsafe.
Document a complaint.

questions.rationale: Professional disagreement should begin with facts and structured communication.

questions.stem: An assistant performs delegated observations but fails to report a concerning change. What should the registered nurse review?

options.text: Only the assistant's attitude.
The clarity of instructions, reporting parameters, supervision and competence.
Whether the patient complained.
Only the observation form.

questions.rationale: Delegation failures may reflect both individual and system factors.

questions.stem: Which statement about delegation is correct?

options.text: Delegation transfers accountability completely.
Any task may be delegated if the ward is busy.
The nurse remains accountable for selecting, directing, supervising and evaluating delegated care.
Role titles are equivalent across countries.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability remains with the delegating nurse for the delegation process.

questions.stem: A patient's rights are threatened by an organisational process. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the process because it is policy.
Tell the patient nothing can be done.
Ignore the issue unless harm occurs.
Raise the concern through appropriate advocacy and escalation channels.

questions.rationale: Advocacy may require challenging systems that threaten rights.

questions.stem: Which action best manages professional disagreement?

options.text: Structured communication using evidence and patient needs.
Personal criticism.
Avoidance.
Public confrontation.

questions.rationale: Professional conflict should remain respectful and evidence-based.

questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether a local support-worker category may administer medication. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume equivalence with the previous country.
Verify the local role and policy before delegating.
Ask the worker what they usually do.
Delegate only simple medicines.

questions.rationale: Role titles and responsibilities differ across jurisdictions.

questions.stem: A delegated task becomes inappropriate because the patient's condition becomes unstable. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Allow completion to avoid confusion.
Ask the worker to make the decision.
Reassess the patient and revise or withdraw the delegation.
Document the change after the shift.

questions.rationale: Delegation must be reconsidered when circumstances change.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects interprofessional accountability?

options.text: Each profession works independently.
The most senior clinician carries all accountability.
Conflict is avoided.
Roles are clear, concerns are communicated respectfully and unresolved risks are escalated.

questions.rationale: Accountability within teams requires role clarity and communication. Section 4 - Cultural Safety, Privacy and Professional Communication

questions.stem: A patient with limited English is asked to sign consent using a relative as interpreter. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Pause and arrange a professional interpreter before the decision.
Proceed because the relative knows the patient.
Ask the relative to sign instead.
Provide a leaflet and obtain the signature.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation is required for complex or high-risk information when accuracy and confidentiality matter.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates cultural safety?

options.text: Treating every patient identically.
Using self-awareness, respectful enquiry and attention to how the patient experiences care.
Relying on cultural stereotypes.
Avoiding discussion of beliefs.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety is determined through respectful, individualised care rather than assumptions.

questions.stem: A patient declines a care practice for cultural reasons that do not create safety concerns. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Insist on the routine.
Document non-compliance.
Explore and accommodate the preference where possible.
Ask family to persuade the patient.

questions.rationale: Cultural respect should be accommodated when clinically safe.

questions.stem: Which situation requires a professional interpreter most clearly?

options.text: A simple greeting.
Choosing a meal.
Asking the room temperature.
A complex consent or high-risk treatment discussion.

questions.rationale: Accuracy and confidentiality are critical in complex or high-risk discussions.

questions.stem: A family member answers every question for a capable patient. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Address the patient directly, explore preferences and ensure an opportunity for independent participation.
Accept the arrangement automatically.
Exclude the family immediately.
Ask the family to sign all forms.

questions.rationale: Power differences can limit participation; the nurse should support the patient's own voice.

questions.stem: Which practice best protects digital confidentiality?

options.text: Using personal messaging for convenience.
Using secure approved systems and sharing only necessary information.
Sharing passwords during busy shifts.
Leaving records open for team access.

questions.rationale: Electronic communication requires secure access and appropriate sharing.

questions.stem: A nurse sends patient details to the wrong email address. What should happen?

options.text: Delete the sent message and do nothing else.
Ask the recipient to ignore it.
Follow the organisation's privacy-breach reporting and containment process immediately.
Wait to see whether harm occurs.

questions.rationale: Digital breaches require prompt containment and reporting.

questions.stem: Which statement about family interpreters is correct?

options.text: They are always preferable because they know the patient.
They may interpret any legal discussion.
They remove the need to check understanding.
They may support the patient but should not replace qualified interpretation when accuracy or confidentiality matters.

questions.rationale: Professional interpreters provide accuracy, neutrality and confidentiality.

questions.stem: A patient says a care interaction felt culturally unsafe even though staff followed policy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Listen, reflect on power and communication, and explore how care could be improved.
Explain that policy proves the care was safe.
Dismiss the concern as subjective.
Ask the family to explain the culture.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety includes the patient's experience, not merely staff intention.

questions.stem: Which handover feature makes responsibility clear?

options.text: A general statement that the patient is stable.
Structured information including current risks, actions, outstanding tasks and who is responsible.
A diagnosis list only.
Informal conversation without confirmation.

questions.rationale: Structured handover should make risk and ownership visible.

questions.stem: What is closed-loop communication?

options.text: A written message without response.
A confidential discussion.
The receiver repeats the message and the sender confirms it.
A handover completed by one person.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop communication verifies that a message was heard and understood correctly.

questions.stem: A verbal order is unclear during an emergency. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Guess based on experience.
Ask another nurse later.
Document the order after administration.
Read back the order and seek confirmation before acting.

questions.rationale: Read-back reduces misunderstanding in high-risk communication.

questions.stem: A patient requests that sensitive information not be shared with family. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respect confidentiality unless disclosure is legally required for safety.
Share it because family support is important.
Tell the family indirectly.
Ask another clinician to disclose it.

questions.rationale: Patient preferences and privacy should be respected within legal limits.

questions.stem: Which action best supports communication across cultures?

options.text: Assuming silence means agreement.
Checking understanding through teach-back and asking what matters to the patient.
Using only written information.
Speaking more loudly.

questions.rationale: Understanding should be confirmed, and preferences should be explored directly.

questions.stem: A remote consultation takes place while other people can overhear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue because the patient joined voluntarily.
Avoid documenting the consultation.
Check privacy and arrange a safer alternative if needed.
Ask others to remain quiet.

questions.rationale: Remote care requires active protection of privacy.

questions.stem: A patient's cultural preference conflicts with an immediate safety requirement. What is the best approach?

options.text: Ignore the preference.
Follow the preference regardless of risk.
Ask security to intervene immediately.
Explain the safety concern respectfully and seek the least intrusive acceptable alternative.

questions.rationale: Cultural respect does not remove safety responsibilities, but alternatives should be explored.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates culturally safe communication?

options.text: The patient can participate, understands information and feels respected rather than stereotyped.
The nurse avoids offence.
The family agrees with the plan.
An interpreter is used for every interaction.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety focuses on the person's experience and meaningful participation.

questions.stem: A handover omits who will follow up an abnormal result. What is the main risk?

options.text: The handover is too short.
Responsibility may be unclear and necessary action may be missed.
The patient may ask questions.
Documentation becomes repetitive.

questions.rationale: Clear ownership is essential across teams.

questions.stem: Which action best protects confidentiality during verbal communication?

options.text: Discussing patient details in a staff cafeteria.
Using initials in a public place.
Using an appropriate private setting and limiting information to those involved in care.
Speaking quietly in a lift.

questions.rationale: Privacy depends on both audience and setting.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects professional international communication?

options.text: The nurse uses one standard style for everyone.
Family members interpret all discussions.
Digital communication is used whenever convenient.
Communication is culturally safe, secure, structured and clear about responsibility.

questions.rationale: International professionalism integrates cultural safety, privacy and reliable team communication.
